386.title: "As is his desire, so is his will; as his will, so his deed" (4.4)
386.hook: January's gym crowd thins out by March, and a line from the Upanishad looks one step further back
386.tomorrow: neti, neti — the great unborn self
386.howItsDone: Hindu teachers cite this verse to explain karma as growing from desire and intention, not only from outward acts; the line about letting go of the heart's desires (4.4.7) also appears in the Katha Upanishad.

segments.voice: Yesterday, death in the Brihadaranyaka: a caterpillar at the tip of a blade, reaching for the next before letting go. Your line was the leaf. Did you notice yourself reaching before you let go? Day three hundred eighty-six.

In January, the gym fills up. New shoes, new plans, a firm decision. By March, a lot of the new faces are gone. It usually isn't for lack of information. Plenty of them knew what to do. They made a resolution, and it didn't hold. Yajnavalkya, still talking with King Janaka about what happens after death, stops to explain where a life actually comes from, and it isn't where the January crowd starts. It's one step further back.
screen: `JANUARY: THE GYM IS FULL.` → `MARCH: IT'S EMPTY.` → `ONE STEP FURTHER BACK.`

segments.voice: As a person acts, he says, as a person behaves, so they become. Doing good, one becomes good. Doing harm, one becomes harmful. That's the karma we heard about privately with Artabhaga, now said out loud to a king. But then he goes deeper. Some say, he adds, a person is made of desire. And here's the line: yathakamo bhavati tat kratur bhavati. As is the desire, so is the will. As is the will, so is the deed. As is the deed, so is what one becomes. Four steps. Desire, the wanting underneath. Kratu, the will or resolve, the decision you make. The deed, the thing you actually do. And what you reach, what you turn into. The January crowd starts at step two, the resolution, and wonders why it doesn't hold. The text says the resolution grows out of what you actually want. Then Yajnavalkya follows it past death. The one who still desires goes on, carried by the deed to what the mind clung to, and when that's spent, comes back to act again. But the one who doesn't desire, whose only desire is the self, doesn't wander. And then a verse the Katha Upanishad shares: when all the desires that live in the heart are let go, the mortal becomes immortal, and reaches Brahman, here. And the body? It lies like a snake's old skin on an anthill, dead and cast off. Notice the order the text insists on: the wanting comes first, and everything else grows out of it.
screen: `AS ONE ACTS, SO ONE BECOMES.` · `A PERSON IS MADE OF DESIRE.` · `DESIRE, WILL, DEED, WHAT YOU REACH.` · `THE SNAKE'S OLD SKIN.` · then, large: `DESIRE → WILL → DEED → DESTINY.`

segments.voice: Two minutes going one step back. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you did today, small or large. Ask: what did I decide that made me do it? Then go one step further: what did I want, underneath the decision? Don't judge the want. Just find it. If it surprises you, notice that. Then rest, and let the wanting be seen. The bell holds the time.
Kratu, will, resolve, purpose. The step between what you want and what you do: as the desire, so the kratu.
Your line: desire, will, deed, destiny. Today, before one decision, ask what you actually want, and see whether the decision changes. Day three hundred eighty-six.

387.title: Neti, neti — the great unborn self (4.4–4.5)
387.hook: one word, said twice: a description of the self that works by refusing
387.tomorrow: the peace chant — purnam adah, purnam idam — from fullness, fullness
387.howItsDone: Neti neti is used as a method of inquiry in Advaita Vedanta, where students set aside body, breath and mind as not the self; other Vedanta schools read the phrase as denying any limit to Brahman.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kratu — as is his desire, so is his will; as his will, so his deed. Desire, will, deed, destiny. Did one decision change when you asked what you actually wanted? Day three hundred eighty-seven.
screen: `KRATU — AS IS HIS DESIRE, SO IS HIS WILL.`

segments.voice: Neti, neti. Not this, not this. One word, said twice. It's a description that works by refusing to describe. It's been woven through the book. It's in the chapter where Shakalya lost his head. It's much earlier, too, in book two. And it comes back at the high point of Yajnavalkya's talk with King Janaka, later in the same talk as the snake's old skin, when he's ready to say who the self really is.
screen: `NETI, NETI.` → `NOT THIS, NOT THIS.` → `A DESCRIPTION THAT REFUSES.`

segments.voice: He is the great unborn self, Yajnavalkya says, the one made of knowing among the senses. He lies in the space within the heart, ruler of all, lord of all. He doesn't grow greater by good deeds, or smaller by bad ones. People seek him through study, through ritual, through giving, through fasting. Knowing him, one becomes a sage. Longing for him, wanderers leave home. And then: sa esha neti neti atma. That self is not this, not this. He can't be grasped, for he is never grasped. He can't be destroyed, for he is never destroyed. He doesn't cling, for he never clings. He is unbound; he doesn't tremble; he isn't harmed. In book two the text had already said why this is the highest teaching: there is nothing higher than this not. Here's the logic. Everything you can name is something seen, and Ushasta learned you can't see the seer. So every name falls short. Not the body. Not the breath. Not the mind. Not the dream, not even deep sleep. Each not clears a little more room. Hindu schools hear these two words differently. Shankara, in Advaita, hears them refusing every description, because Brahman is beyond all qualities. Ramanuja hears them saying not only this: Brahman isn't limited to anything just described, because its good qualities have no end. Both take the words seriously. And in book four, after the book tells the whole Maitreyi conversation one more time, it says simply: having said this, Yajnavalkya went away. The man who left finally leaves.
screen: `THE GREAT UNBORN SELF.` · `UNGRASPED, UNHARMED, UNBOUND.` · `NOTHING HIGHER THAN THIS NOT.` · `BEYOND ALL QUALITIES, OR NOT ONLY THIS?` · then, large: `NOT THIS, NOT THIS.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with the names you carry. Sit, and breathe. Let the labels you use for yourself come up one at a time: a name, a job, a role in a family, a mood from today. Give each one a breath, and as the breath goes out, say inwardly: not this. Not to throw it away; each one is real. Just, in the text's terms, not the self. Then rest with its last words: unbound, unharmed, not trembling. The bell holds the time.
Neti. Na iti: not so, not this. In the Brihadaranyaka, said twice, the way the self is described by refusing every description.
Your line: not this, not this. Today, when you catch yourself saying I am my job, my mood or my mistake, answer quietly: not this. Day three hundred eighty-seven.

388.title: The peace chant — purnam adah, purnam idam — from fullness, fullness (5.1)
388.hook: light a candle from a candle and the first flame loses nothing: the great line we leave the Brihadaranyaka on, chanted all over the world
388.tomorrow: the teacher's charge to the student: "speak the truth, practice dharma"
388.howItsDone: The purnam adah chant is recited as the shanti mantra of the Isha Upanishad and of the Shukla Yajurveda tradition, at the start and end of study, at pujas and at many gatherings, followed by om shanti, shanti, shanti.

segments.voice: Yesterday, neti, neti: not this, not this, and Yajnavalkya finally went away. Did you answer not this to a job, a mood or a mistake? Day three hundred eighty-eight.

Light a candle. Now use it to light a second one. Look at the first flame. It hasn't gotten any smaller. Light ten more from it, a hundred, and it's still exactly as bright. Something was given away completely, and nothing was lost. If you've ever been to a Hindu gathering, a yoga class, or the start of an Upanishad recital, you may have heard a short chant in Sanskrit that ends om shanti, shanti, shanti. That chant comes from the Brihadaranyaka, at the opening of its fifth book, and it's where we leave the book.
screen: `A CANDLE LIGHTS A CANDLE.` → `THE FIRST FLAME LOSES NOTHING.` → `A CHANT HEARD AT THE START OF STUDY.`

segments.voice: Here it is. Purnam adah purnam idam purnat purnam udacyate, purnasya purnam adaya purnam evavashishyate. That is full. This is full. From the full, the full comes forth. Take the full from the full, and the full alone remains. Purna means full, whole, complete, lacking nothing. That is the far side, Brahman beyond everything you can point to. This is the near side, the world right here, the one you're sitting in. And the chant refuses to make either one the lesser half. The world doesn't come out of Brahman like a slice out of a cake, leaving a hole. It comes out like a flame from a flame. People who love mathematics sometimes hear infinity in it: take infinity from infinity, and infinity is left. The tradition attaches it as the peace chant of the Isha Upanishad, too, and it's chanted at the start of study, worship and gatherings. And it's a fitting place to finish the Brihadaranyaka. Look back down this great forest of a book. The horse that was the whole cosmos. Death's hunger making a world. The breath the demons couldn't pierce. I am, then fear, then longing. The self split into two halves. Maitreyi setting aside the earth. Salt with no inside or outside. Honey for each other. A thousand cows, challenger after challenger, a head that fell. The light of the self, the dreamer, deep sleep, the caterpillar, desire. Not this, not this. And at the end, not emptiness. Fullness. Tomorrow, a new Upanishad, the Taittiriya, and a teacher's speech to his graduating students.
screen: `THAT IS FULL. THIS IS FULL.` · `A FLAME FROM A FLAME, NOT A SLICE.` · `THE PEACE CHANT OF STUDY AND WORSHIP.` · `THE WHOLE FOREST OF A BOOK.` · then, large: `FULL FROM FULL.`

segments.voice: Two minutes of fullness. Sit, and breathe. On the in-breath, let the word come: full. On the out-breath: full. See whether the breath you just gave away left you lacking anything; the next one is already arriving. If you'd like, say the chant silently, or just its first line: purnam adah, purnam idam. Let the line and the breath move together until the words fall away. The bell holds the time.
Purna, full, whole, complete. In the peace chant, what that is, what this is, and what remains when the full is taken from the full.
Your line: full from full. Today, give something away completely, time, attention, a good word, and notice whether you're any less. Day three hundred eighty-eight.

389.title: The teacher's charge to the student: "speak the truth, practice dharma" (1.11)
389.hook: one of the oldest graduation speeches in the world, and its most surprising line: copy our good deeds, not the others
389.tomorrow: "honor your mother as god, your father as god, your teacher, your guest"
389.howItsDone: The teacher's charge in Taittiriya 1.11 is recited in traditional Vedic schools at the end of study, and satyam vada, dharmam chara is widely quoted in Indian schools and at graduation ceremonies.

segments.voice: Yesterday, purna: the end of our time in the Brihadaranyaka: that is full, this is full. Your line was full from full. Did you give something away and find yourself no less? Day three hundred eighty-nine.

Caps, gowns, a stage, and someone at a podium telling a room full of graduates how to live. Graduation speeches are mostly forgotten by dinner. Here's one that's lasted well over two thousand years. It's in a new Upanishad, the Taittiriya. A teacher has finished teaching the Veda to his student, years of it, line by line. The student is about to leave and start a life. And before he goes, the teacher stands up and gives him his charge.
screen: `CAPS, GOWNS, A PODIUM.` → `A NEW UPANISHAD.` → `THE TEACHER STANDS UP.`

segments.voice: First, the book. The Taittiriya belongs to the Black Yajurveda. A later legend explains its odd name, tittiri, partridges: when Yajnavalkya, our friend from the Brihadaranyaka, quarreled with his teacher and gave back what he'd learned, his fellow students took the form of partridges and gathered it up. Now the speech. It opens with three short commands that many Hindus know by heart: satyam vada, dharmam chara. Speak the truth. Practice dharma. And don't neglect your study. Then the practical part. Bring your teacher the gift he'd value. Don't let your family line be cut off. Don't drift from the truth, from dharma, from what keeps you well, from your own flourishing, from learning and teaching. And then a line you might not expect from a teacher. Whatever deeds of ours are blameless, those you should follow, not the others. Whatever good conduct is ours, honor that, not the rest. The teacher is admitting, at the graduation, that he isn't perfect. Copy my good deeds, not the others. And one more, for every hard moment after graduation. If you're ever in doubt about what to do, he says, look at the people there who are wise, devoted, and gentle, and do as they would do. Then the teacher seals it. This is the command. This is the teaching. This is the secret of the Veda. The secret of the Veda, after all those years, turns out to be: tell the truth, do what's right, keep learning, and copy the best of the people who taught you.
screen: `THE TAITTIRIYA: THE PARTRIDGES' BOOK.` · `SPEAK THE TRUTH. PRACTICE DHARMA.` · `FOLLOW OUR GOOD DEEDS, NOT THE OTHERS.` · `IN DOUBT? LOOK AT THE WISE AND GENTLE.` · then, large: `THE GRADUATION SPEECH.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with your teachers. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who taught you something that mattered: a teacher, a parent, a coach, a boss, a grandparent. Let one of their good deeds come to mind, something worth copying. Then, gently, let one of their flaws come too. Hold both without judging. Then let the flaw go, and keep the good deed. Rest with that. The bell holds the time.
Satyam vada, speak the truth. The first words of the teacher's charge, as the student leaves to start a life.
Your line: the graduation speech. Today, do one good thing you learned from someone who taught you, and leave their flaw where it is. Day three hundred eighty-nine.

390.title: "Honor your mother as god, your father as god, your teacher, your guest" (1.11)
390.hook: a line on airport posters and kitchen walls, and where it really comes from
390.howItsDone: Many Hindus honor parents and elders by touching their feet for a blessing, honor teachers on Guru Purnima, and treat a guest as a form of the divine, offering food and water first.

segments.voice: Yesterday, satyam vada: speak the truth, practice dharma, follow our good deeds and not the others. Your line was the graduation speech. Which good thing from a teacher did you do? Day three hundred ninety.

Fly into India and you may well see three Sanskrit words on a poster: atithi devo bhava. The guest is god. India's tourism posters have used them. You can also find the same words, or their neighbors, framed on kitchen walls. They're much older than any poster. They're from the very same graduation speech as yesterday, the next part of the teacher's charge, and the guest isn't even first on the list.
screen: `ATITHI DEVO BHAVA.` → `ON A TOURISM POSTER.` → `FROM THE SAME GRADUATION SPEECH.`

segments.voice: Here's the list, in order. Matri devo bhava. Pitri devo bhava. Acharya devo bhava. Atithi devo bhava. Mother first, then father, then teacher, then guest. The grammar is lovely. It isn't quite treat your mother like a god. It's be someone for whom the mother is a god. It's describing the kind of person the student is leaving to become. And notice who's on it. Two people who gave you life. One who gave you learning. And then a stranger at the door. Tradition explains atithi as someone who comes without a set day, unannounced, and they go on the same list as your parents. Then, right after, the teacher turns to giving. Give with faith; don't give without faith. Give generously. Give with modesty. Give with a little awe, worried it's not enough. Give with understanding. Five ways to hand something over, and not one of them is give when you feel like it. Does as god mean obey without question? The charge itself answers that. In the very next breath, the same teacher says: follow our blameless deeds, not the others. Honor isn't blind. Hindu families live this out in many ways: touching a parent's or elder's feet for a blessing, a festival day for teachers, guru purnima, and a plate of food for whoever turns up. The list begins at home and ends at the front door, with whoever happens to be standing there.
screen: `MOTHER, FATHER, TEACHER, GUEST.` · `BE ONE FOR WHOM THE MOTHER IS GOD.` · `THE GUEST: NO SET DAY.` · `GIVE WITH FAITH, GRACE, MODESTY.` · then, large: `MATRI DEVO BHAVA.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with the four. Sit, and breathe. Bring your mother to mind, or whoever mothered you, living or gone. Let one breath be for her. Then your father, or whoever fathered you: one breath. Then a teacher: one breath. Then a guest, someone who once turned up unexpectedly in your life: one breath. If any of these is painful, keep the breath and let the face blur. Then rest. The bell holds the time.
Atithi, guest. Mother, father, teacher, and the guest at the door: four for whom the student is charged to be someone who sees them as a god.
Your line: matri devo bhava. Today, call or message your mother, or someone who mothered you, or, if no one's left to call, say thank you out loud. Day three hundred ninety.

391.title: The five sheaths: food (2.1)
391.hook: a set of nesting dolls, and the outermost one is made of last week's dinners
391.howItsDone: Many Hindus offer food to God before eating and receive it back as prasad; in Vedanta and in yoga teaching, the five koshas drawn from this Upanishad are used to describe the layers of a person, starting with the body made of food.

segments.voice: Yesterday: matri devo bhava, pitri devo bhava, acharya devo bhava, atithi devo bhava. Mother, father, teacher, guest. Did you reach someone who mothered you? Day three hundred ninety-one.

Open a set of nesting dolls. Inside the big painted one, a smaller one. Inside that, a smaller one. You keep going, and the dolls get smaller and finer, until you reach the last, tiny one in the middle. The Taittiriya Upanishad's second book takes a person apart the same way, five layers deep. Over the next three days we'll open them one by one. Today, the outermost doll. And it's made of something you ate this week.
screen: `A DOLL INSIDE A DOLL.` → `FIVE LAYERS DEEP.` → `THE OUTERMOST IS MADE OF FOOD.`

segments.voice: The book opens with a promise: the one who knows Brahman reaches the highest. And a definition in four Sanskrit words: satyam jnanam anantam brahma. Brahman is truth, knowledge, the infinite. Then a creation story, told like a relay. From this self, space came. From space, wind. From wind, fire. From fire, water. From water, earth. From earth, plants. From plants, food. From food, the person. So the person, the text says, is made of the essence of food. Annamaya: made of food. And it draws that person as a bird. This is the head. This is the right wing. This is the left wing. This is the body. This, underneath, is the tail, the foundation. Then a short hymn to food. From food all creatures are born. By food they live. Into food, in the end, they go. Food is the eldest of beings, so it's called the medicine of everything. Read plainly, it's something you can check. The hands holding your phone were, not long ago, rice, lentils, bread, an apple. And then the text says: different from this one made of food, inside it, is another self, made of breath. That's tomorrow. One more thing. Later Hindu teachers call these layers the five koshas, the five sheaths, like a sword's scabbard. The Taittiriya itself doesn't use that word. It just keeps saying: inside this one, another self.
screen: `SATYAM JNANAM ANANTAM BRAHMA.` · `SPACE, WIND, FIRE, WATER, EARTH, FOOD.` · `THE PERSON MADE OF FOOD, SHAPED LIKE A BIRD.` · `INSIDE IT, ANOTHER SELF.` · then, large: `ANNAMAYA.`

segments.voice: Two minutes in the outermost doll. Sit, and feel the body's weight on the seat. Notice its warmth, its pulse, the heaviness of the hands. Then remember, gently: this was food. Grain, fruit, water, sunlight, a farmer's work, someone's cooking. Let a little thanks go to all of it. Then feel the body again, just as it is, the first layer, the one you can touch. The bell holds the time.
Annamaya, made of food. In the Taittiriya, the outermost self: the body, built from what we eat, and the first of the five layers.
Your line: the medicine of everything. At your next meal, before the first bite, look at the food and remember you're about to become it. Day three hundred ninety-one.

392.title: Breath, mind (2.2–2.3)
392.hook: inside the self made of food, the Taittiriya finds another self, made of breath, and inside that, one made of mind
392.howItsDone: Many Hindus learn the Taittiriya's five layers through Vedanta study and yoga teaching, where breath practice (pranayama) is described as working on the pranamaya layer between body and mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the five sheaths, and the first of them. Your line was the medicine of everything, the self made of food. Did you look at a meal and see your own body in it? Day three hundred ninety-two, the end of week fifty-six.

A rough experiment, the kind you've already run without meaning to. A person can go a long while without food, a much shorter while without water, and hardly any time without breath. So which one is holding you together right now? The body you can see is made of lunch. But something is moving through that body again and again, quietly, whether you remember it or not. And riding on top of the breath, there's a third thing: the running commentary in your head that may, at this moment, be wondering where this is going. The Taittiriya Upanishad noticed all three, and it put them in order. Yesterday it gave you the outer one. Today it goes two layers in.
screen: `A WHILE WITHOUT FOOD. NO TIME WITHOUT BREATH.` → `THE COMMENTARY IN YOUR HEAD.` → `TWO LAYERS IN.`

segments.voice: Chapter two, section two. After the self made of food, the text says: different from this, and inside it, is another self, made of breath. Pranamaya. And it adds a detail. The outer self is filled by this one, and this one too has the shape of a person. So the layers aren't like an onion's skins sitting side by side. They're more like water filling a vessel, taking its shape from the inside. Then the text draws the breath-self like a bird. Prana, the in-breath, is its head. Vyana, the breath that spreads through the body, is one wing. Apana, the down-going breath, is the other. Space is its body, and the earth is its tail, the thing it rests on. And it says why breath matters: prano hi bhutanam ayuh. Breath is the life-span of all beings. Gods, people and animals all breathe after it. Section three goes in again. Inside the breath-self is a self made of mind. Manomaya. And here the bird is drawn out of scripture. The Yajur Veda is its head. The Rig Veda is one wing, the Sama Veda the other. Teaching is its body, and the hymns of the Atharvans are its tail. It's a surprising picture. The mind in this text isn't only a stream of thoughts. It's shaped by the words a person has learned, recited, and carried. And then, as before, the text points inward once more: inside this one, another self. That's tomorrow.
screen: `INSIDE FOOD, A SELF MADE OF BREATH.` · `EACH LAYER FILLS THE ONE OUTSIDE IT.` · `BREATH IS THE LIFE-SPAN OF BEINGS.` · `INSIDE BREATH, A SELF MADE OF MIND.` · then, large: `PRANAMAYA. MANOMAYA.`

segments.voice: Two layers, two minutes. Sit, and start with the body: its weight, the self made of food. Then go one layer in. Feel the breath arrive and leave without steering it. Notice how it fills the body from the inside, belly, ribs, the back of the throat. That's pranamaya. Then go one layer in again. Watch what the mind is doing on top of the breath: a word, a plan, a memory, a tune. Don't chase it. Just notice that it rides on the breath, the way the text draws it. The bell holds the time.
Breath. Prana, the life-span of beings, which in the Taittiriya forms a whole self inside the body, with the self made of mind inside it.

Your line: pranamaya, manomaya. Today, the next time your mind races, check your breath first, and see which one changed. And that's week fifty-six: desire and will, not this, not this, full from full, the teacher's charge, honor your mother, food, and breath. Day three hundred ninety-two.
screen: `WEEK FIFTY-SIX: DESIRE · NETI NETI · FULLNESS · THE CHARGE · MOTHER AS GOD · FOOD · BREATH`
